title: TresInd Studio Holds Onto Three Michelin Stars, Keeping Indian Dining at Dubai's Summit
excerpt: The Palm Jumeirah restaurant retained its three stars in the fifth Michelin Guide Dubai, cementing its standing as the highest-rated Indian restaurant in the world.
body:
• Trèsind Studio retained its Three Michelin Stars in the 2026 Michelin Guide Dubai — the fifth edition, unveiled this week — standing alongside FZN by Björn Frantzén as the city's only two three-star restaurants.
  • Chef Himanshu Saini's tasting-menu concept at the St. Regis Gardens on Palm Jumeirah was the first Indian restaurant anywhere in the world to win three Michelin stars, a distinction it first earned in 2025.
  • The 2026 selection, which has nearly doubled since the guide's 2022 debut, promoted Orfali Bros to two stars and added newcomers Birch and KIGO at one star, taking the one-star list to 14 restaurants.
  • The dining room books out months in advance and the tasting menu runs about AED 1,250 per person — if a Dubai trip is on the calendar, reserve early through the restaurant's website.

Trèsind Studio has held its place at the very top of world gastronomy. In the fifth edition of the Michelin Guide Dubai, unveiled this week, the Palm Jumeirah restaurant retained its Three Michelin Stars — a distinction it first earned in 2025 as the first Indian restaurant anywhere to reach that level. Only two restaurants in Dubai hold three stars: Trèsind Studio and FZN by Björn Frantzén.

Context and background

Trèsind Studio is the creative vision of chef Himanshu Saini, a protégé of Manish Mehrotra of Indian Accent fame, working out of the St. Regis Gardens on Palm Jumeirah. The concept is tasting-menu-only, split into vegetarian and non-vegetarian journeys that run through India's landscapes, seasons and cultural narratives with theatrical, modernist presentation — chaat, lentils and regional curries reinterpreted with unexpected textures while staying rooted in Indian flavour.

"And for parents fielding questions from curious non-Indian friends about what Indian food "really" is, the answer now comes with three stars attached."

The three stars were only the beginning of a remarkable 2026 for the restaurant: it scored 93.50 on La Liste, won the Chefs' Choice Award at the World's 50 Best MENA, and was named the Best Restaurant in the Middle East at the World's 50 Best Restaurants. This week's guide also promoted Orfali Bros to two stars — an evolution, the guide noted, from neighbourhood bistro into a flagship of Middle Eastern gastronomy — while Il Ristorante-Niko Romito, Row on 45 and STAY by Yannick Alléno kept theirs. Newcomers Birch and KIGO each earned one star, and four new Bib Gourmands brought that list to 22.

Impact and analysis

The headline is bigger than one dining room: Indian cuisine now sits at the top tables of the world as a matter of course, not exception. The ecosystem around Trèsind Studio is flourishing — Gaggan in Bangkok, helmed by Gaggan Anand, remains a powerhouse of progressive Indian cooking; Masque in Mumbai, ranked No. 15 on Asia's 50 Best Restaurants 2026, won the Art of Hospitality Award, the first for an Indian restaurant; and Manish Mehrotra himself opened Nisaba in New Delhi earlier this year. Michelin stars for Indian restaurants now stretch across the US, UK, UAE and Asia.

What has changed is the vocabulary. The chefs leading this wave have moved beyond butter chicken and generic curry toward regional diversity, hyper-local sourcing and personal narrative — a shift Indian diners, who know the difference between a Moirang Phee and a Saphee Lanphee, have long been waiting to see rewarded.

Diaspora angle

For the large Indian community in the UAE, Trèsind Studio's retention of three stars is a point of uncomplicated pride: the highest-rated Indian restaurant on the planet sits in Dubai, a city many of them call home. For NRIs visiting family in the Gulf, it has become the reservation to book — the tasting is a showcase of how far the cuisine travels when it is taken seriously. And for parents fielding questions from curious non-Indian friends about what Indian food "really" is, the answer now comes with three stars attached.

What's next

The question for next year's guide is whether another Indian restaurant joins the starred ranks — and whether Trèsind Studio can extend a run that already includes the MENA Chefs' Choice and the Middle East's top restaurant title. Saini's mentor Mehrotra, with the newly opened Nisaba, is part of the same conversation. For diners, the practical note stands: with the room booking out months ahead and a menu at about AED 1,250 per person, the planning starts now.
